BEFORE THE NEW MEXICO PUBLIC REGULATION COMMISSION
IN THE MATTER OF SOUTHWESTERN PUBLIC                         )
SERVICE COMPANY’S APPLICATION FOR: (1)                       )
REVISION OF ITS RETAIL RATES UNDER                           )
ADVICE NOTICE 341; AND (2) OTHER                             )
ASSOCIATED RELIEF.                                           )      CASE NO. 25-00079-UT
                                                             )
SOUTHWESTERN PUBLIC SERVICE COMPANY,                         )
                                                             )
APPLICANT.                                                   )

         LOUSIANA ENERGY SERVICES' AND FEDERAL EXECUTIVE AGENCIES'
                              RESPONSE BRIEF

            Intervenors Louisiana Energy Services, L.L.C. ("LES") and the Federal Executive

 Agencies ("FEA") hereby jointly submit to the New Mexico Public Regulation Commission

 ("Commission" or "NMPRC") their Response Brief pursuant to the Hearing Examiners' Order on

 Post-Hearing Briefing issued on July 28, 2026, and 1.2.2.36 NMAC.

            The key contention in this case is Utility Division Staff's ("Staff") opposition to the

 Comprehensive Stipulation ("Stipulation") joined in or not opposed by all other parties in this case.

 Staff's Post-Hearing Brief ("Staff Brief") raised no new issues or arguments, but simply reiterated

 its positions that were already addressed in testimony and rebutted in other parties' testimonies and

 initial briefs. LES-FEA's Initial Post-Hearing Brief ("LES-FEA Initial Brief") reiterated the legal

 standards the Commission applies to such Stipulations,1 reviewed the terms of the Stipulation,2

 rebutted Staff's objections,3 and addressed the Hearing Examiners' questions;4 and those points are



 1
     LES-FEA Initial Brief at 2-5.
 2
     Id. at 5-13.
 3
     Id. at 13-22.
 4
     Id.at 22-23.
 incorporated by reference herein. Rather than repeating those arguments, this Response Brief

provides short responses and references to previous briefing and testimony on Staff's key positions.

                                                 RESPONSE

           1.       Staff's Proposed Cap on the Deferred Tax Asset ("DTA") for Production Tax
                    Credits ("PTC") is Unreasonably Long

           Staff recommends a ten-year cap on the DTA, with a notification to customers after two

years.5 This is an unreasonably long period of time and could lead to accumulation of excessive

carrying charges for which customers would pay. LES and FEA, along with other parties, proposed

that, within 365 days after generating a transfer-eligible PTC, SPS would transfer the credit or stop

accruing carrying charges on any remaining balance in the DTA. 6 This recommendation is

reasonable to ensure that PTCs accrued in a DTA by SPS do not carry forward for an unreasonable

amount of time. The proposed limit of 365 days provides double the average time to sell the PTCs

and is more protective for customers than Staff's proposal. Even SPS's proposal of a two-year cap7

is more protective for customers than Staff's outlier position. Staff's recommendation would not

result in just and reasonable rates and should be rejected.

           2.       Staff's Proposed Allocation of PTCs is Contrary to Cost Causation Principles

           Staff asserts the PTC allocation should not follow well-established cost causation

principles.8 That position is not supportable and is unreasonable for the reasons explained by LES




5
    Staff Brief at 8.
6
    LES-FEA Initial Brief at 22.
7
    SPS's Initial Post-Hearing Brief ("SPS Brief") at 36.
8
    Staff Brief at 10-11.


                                                       2
 and FEA, and other parties, and should be rejected.9 The allocation of PTCs at energy sources is

fair and reasonable for at least two reasons. First, PTCs are created by energy generation from

renewable resources, so the allocation aligns with how PTCs are created based on customer class

energy demands. Second, the fixed costs of the renewable production resources from which the

PTCs are generated are allocated based on the combination of: 1) customers' average energy

demands and 2) the additional capacity needed to ensure service reliability.10

           3.      Staff's Arguments Regarding Use of Future Test Year are Misplaced

           Staff's first objection to SPS's use of a Future Test Year is that SPS's load forecasts and

resources have changed since the rate application was filed in November 2025.11 Staff appears to

assume that a utility's loads and resources would be cast in stone and unchanging during the course

of a rate case. Such an assumption is unrealistic and unreasonable, and applying such a standard

would result in constant repetitive updates that would render a 9-month or 12-month rate case

untenable. The statutory standard is that the Commission sets rates based on a future test year that

"best reflects" (not perfectly reflects) "the conditions to be experienced during the period when the

rates determined by the commission take effect."12

           Staff also argues at length that the Commission's rulings in Case No. 25-00066-UT

regarding future rate cases applies to this case and supports disapproval of the Stipulation. SPS

filed its rate case application in this case in November 2025. The Commission's Final Order in

Case No. 25-00066-UT was not issued until May 7, 2026. At that time, this case was already


9
    LES-FEA Initial Brief at 23; see also SPS Brief at 39-40.
10
     Id.
11
     Staff Brief at 13-14.
12
     NMSA 1978, § 62-6-14.D.


                                                      3
 pending for six months and was not a "future rate case." Staff's future test year arguments do not

make sense, are not consistent with New Mexico law, and should be rejected.

          4.       The Resolution for Staff's Complaints about Use of a Future Test Year is with
                   the Legislature

          Staff appears to object in general to the use of a future test year in a rate case in New

Mexico while Texas does not allow for future test years. The effect – or lack of effect – of this

difference on rates between SPS's New Mexico and Texas jurisdictions was addressed by several

witnesses in testimony.13 New Mexico law provides for the use of a future test year.14 If the

Commission wishes to eliminate the statutory authority for utilities to file future test year rate

cases, the remedy is with the Legislature.

          5.       Staff's Affordability Arguments are Contrary to Cost of Service Ratemaking
                   Principles

          Staff's view appears to be that the proposed increase to residential class rates, which is

consistent with the cost to serve residential customers but is more than the increase assigned to

certain other classes, is de facto unreasonable and not "affordable." Staff uses the term "affordable"

generally but does not define it or explain how it determined how any particular increase is or is

not "affordable" for a particular rate class. Staff fails to explain why the Stipulation rates are

unreasonable since they are based on long-standing cost of service principles and apply gradualism

to avoid rate shock.15 The New Mexico Department of Justice also advocates on behalf of

residential and small commercial customers, and is a signatory to the Stipulation. There is




13
     See LES-FEA Initial Brief at 13-19 and citations to hearing testimony therein.
14
     NMSA 1978, § 62-6-14.D.
15
     LES-FEA Initial Brief at 19-22.


                                                       4
 insufficient evidence in the record that the Stipulation rates would result in rate shock or are

otherwise not just and reasonable.

                                           CONCLUSION

        Staff is the only party that opposed the Stipulation filed in this case. Staff's reasons for its

opposition are not supported by the evidence in this case or New Mexico law. The Commission

should approve the Stipulation because the evidence demonstrates that it is the result of serious

bargaining between knowledgeable entities, including the utility and its customers who will bear

the burden of the rate increase; balances the interests of ratepayers and the utility; is consistent

with well-established regulatory principles; complies with NM law; is in the public interest; and

will result in fair, just and reasonable rates.

Respectfully submitted on August 31, 2026,
